title: Why you won’t get a flying car
gist: Reviewing J. Storrs Hall's 'Where Is My Flying Car?', Noah Smith argues that American 'engineerism' — the belief that if something can be built it should be — misreads both energy history and consumer demand: China's revealed preference for solar over nuclear shows solar won the real-world cost race, and flying cars remain undemanded because most trips don't fall in the 150-500 mile sweet spot where they'd beat cars or planes.

themes.theme: Engineerism as a flawed mental model

insights.claim: Noah Smith defines 'engineerism' as the belief that if a technology can be built, it ought to be built — distinct from Hayek's 'engineering mentality' (society can be designed like a machine) and Morozov's 'technological solutionism' (tech fixes social problems).
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Useful lens for discounting founder/engineer narratives that justify capital-intensive moonshot projects purely on buildability rather than demonstrated demand.
insights.quote: The idea that if a technology can be built, we ought to build it.

insights.claim: Smith identifies three core weaknesses of engineerism: (1) a contrarian reflex that if experts call something impossible it must be possible, (2) treating difficult engineering feats as inherently desirable regardless of demand, and (3) focusing on supply ('can we build this?') instead of demand ('why would anyone want this?').
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A checklist investors can apply to deep-tech/moonshot pitches (fusion, space, flying cars) to separate genuine market opportunities from engineer-driven vanity projects.
insights.quote: It focuses too much on supply and not enough on demand. To many engineers, the most important question is 'Can we build this?', not 'Why would anyone want this?'.
insights.locator: closing section on the biggest pitfall of engineerism

insights.claim: In the long run, technology gets built because human consumers (including governments as consumers of weapons and monuments) want it, not because engineers find it exciting to build.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Reinforces a demand-first framework for evaluating which frontier technologies (space, nuclear, flying cars) will actually attract sustained capital versus stall as engineering curiosities.
insights.quote: the actual future of technology will be driven by parents shopping for diapers

insights.claim: Since the disputed 1989 cold fusion claim, multiple well-funded replication efforts have failed to reproduce it: a Japanese government project (~$20M, 1990s), a Toyota project (~$18M, 1990s), an Electric Power Research Institute project (~$10M, 2000s), a Google project (~$10M, 2010s), and the U.S. government is now funding another ~$10M effort.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Repeated, well-capitalized failure to replicate cold fusion across public and private sectors over 35+ years is strong evidence against treating it as a suppressed but viable energy technology, informing where R&D capital should (not) go.
insights.quote: None of these efforts have reliably reproduced the effect that the two chemists claimed in 1989.

insights.claim: J. Storrs Hall attributes cold fusion's stalled progress to a 'Machiavelli Effect' (vested research interests suppressing a rival field), but Smith argues this doesn't hold because multiple good-faith, well-funded efforts from different countries and both public and private sectors have tried and failed — that isn't what a genuinely marginalized field looks like.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Undercuts a recurring 'suppressed technology' narrative used to justify continued speculative investment in cold fusion.
insights.quote: Multiple optimistic, good-faith research efforts, from various countries, from both the public and private sectors, have each thrown tens of millions of dollars at the idea, despite repeated lack of success. That is just not what a marginalized area of science looks like.

insights.claim: Hall's continued faith in cold fusion despite the evidence reduces the credibility of his other forecasts in the book, including his reliance on speculative nanotechnology to justify rebuilding U.S. infrastructure 'in a few hours.'
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A useful diligence heuristic: one badly-grounded forecast in a futurist thesis should raise skepticism about adjacent forecasts built on similarly thin analysis.
insights.quote: If Hall hadn't gone all-in on cold fusion, I would have probably been less instinctively skeptical of the nanotech sections.

themes.theme: Energy stagnation, dematerialization, and the Henry Adams Curve

insights.claim: U.S. energy use per capita rose smoothly through the 20th century but leveled off in the 1970s (the 'Henry Adams Curve') and has been falling since the turn of the century, even as U.S. per-capita GDP grew roughly 40% over that same post-2000 period.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Directly counters the assumption that GDP growth requires proportional energy growth — a key data point for debates about degrowth, energy transition pacing, and decoupling.
insights.quote: since the turn of the century, even as energy use has fallen, U.S. per capita GDP has grown by 40%!

insights.claim: Around 1970, Americans began spending more on services than on goods, and this gap has widened continuously since — a phenomenon of 'dematerialization' that Smith argues is why economic growth need not exhaust physical resources.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supports a structural thesis that developed economies will keep shifting capital and consumption toward services (health care, entertainment, experiences) rather than physical goods, relevant to sector-allocation calls.
insights.quote: Around 1970, Americans started spending more on services than on goods, and the gap has only grown wider since then

insights.claim: Even China — the country most fixated on manufacturing primacy and willing to override environmental concerns for cheap energy — is showing a similar shift in household consumption toward services, per a cited World Bank chart.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If China's own economy structurally dematerializes despite state preference for manufacturing, this is a bearish signal for perpetual heavy-industry/commodity demand growth even from China.
insights.quote: It's possible that this is just a fundamental feature of human nature.

themes.theme: Nuclear vs. solar: revealed preference over ideology

insights.claim: France gets most of its electricity from nuclear power (since the 1980s) and has dramatically cut carbon emissions as a result, but its electricity still costs 28 cents/kWh versus 18 cents/kWh in the U.S. — nuclear made French power clean but not cheap or abundant.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts the 'nuclear = abundant cheap energy' assumption often used to justify large nuclear capex bets; investors modeling nuclear economics should weight France's real-world cost outcome, not theoretical projections.
insights.quote: France has plenty of nuclear power, but its electricity costs 28 cents per kWh, compared to 18 cents in America.

insights.claim: China has done the best job in the world of driving down nuclear construction costs, yet even there reactor costs are no lower than they were in 2010, per cited 'Energy Bad Boys' data.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Undercuts the thesis that nuclear costs will fall with scale/learning curves the way solar and batteries have — a bearish signal for nuclear-cost-curve bull cases.
insights.quote: China has probably done the best job of bending the nuclear cost curve downward, and even there, reactor costs aren't lower than they were in 2010

insights.claim: Despite China's ability to keep nuclear costs down and its willingness to build nuclear, China is building far more solar capacity than nuclear, because — with cheap batteries solving the intermittency problem — solar has won the real-world technological race against nuclear.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: China's capital-allocation choice functions as a live, ideology-free 'revealed preference' experiment: it favors solar+storage over nuclear for new generation, a strong signal for where global power-generation capex should be expected to flow.
insights.quote: China is ruthlessly focused on growing its economy...it is not swayed by hippie environmentalists...now, China is building solar far faster than it's building nuclear. Why? Because solar has, broadly speaking, won the technological race.

insights.claim: Chinese engineers have embraced the 'electric revolution' with gusto, producing electric cars cheap and high-quality enough to conquer the global auto market, while American engineerism remains fixated on nuclear almost to the exclusion of solar, wind, and EVs.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Identifies a cultural/ideological bias in U.S. engineering and policy circles that may cause continued underinvestment in the solar/battery/EV stack relative to China, a competitiveness risk.
insights.quote: if you talk to American engineers about energy, nine times out of ten it's just nuclear, nuclear, nuclear.
insights.locator: paragraph on Chinese vs. American engineers

insights.claim: Smith's explanation for American engineerism's persistent preference for nuclear over solar despite solar's superior real-world economics is a 'historical grudge': engineers still resent being told in the 1970s-80s that they couldn't build nuclear, and now resist the alternatives (solar, batteries) environmentalists pushed instead.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A cultural/behavioral explanation for a persistent misallocation bias in U.S. energy R&D and policy circles.
insights.quote: My best guess is that this is a historical grudge.
insights.locator: paragraph on why American engineerism longs for nuclear

themes.theme: Why flying cars won't happen soon

insights.claim: EHang's pilotless VTOL craft already provides flying-car-like rides in China but remains authorized only at a few select locations, despite China having built the world's most extensive high-speed rail network — indicating flying cars are demand-constrained, not technology-constrained.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Even in a state willing to fast-track infrastructure, flying-car-type transport hasn't scaled, suggesting the binding constraint globally is demand economics, not regulation or engineering.

insights.claim: Modeling ground cars, flying cars, and airplanes for travel time, flying cars only clearly beat both ground cars and airplanes over an intermediate distance of roughly 150 to 500 miles — the same range where high-speed rail is usually thought to compete effectively.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Defines the narrow addressable-distance band any real flying-car business model would need to target, useful for evaluating eVTOL/UAM startup total addressable market claims.

insights.claim: Young Americans traveled fewer than half as many miles per day in 2022 than they did two decades earlier, per University of California data — evidence that internet/communication technology is substituting for physical travel, reducing the addressable demand for any new transportation technology including flying cars.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A structural demand headwind for any capital-intensive personal-transportation innovation (flying cars, possibly even future auto demand), since digital substitution is already shrinking physical mobility demand among younger cohorts.
insights.quote: Young Americans traveled fewer than half as many miles per day in 2022 as they did two decades earlier
insights.locator: paragraph on communication technology substituting for travel

insights.claim: Hall's argument that flying-car demand would spontaneously create new destinations at the required distances ignores a cold-start problem: without enough flying cars, new destinations can't emerge, and without destinations, owning a flying car is unattractive.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A general critique applicable to any two-sided-market hardware product (also relevant to eVTUAM/air-taxi business models) — supply-side chicken-and-egg problems can permanently suppress adoption absent a forcing mechanism.
insights.quote: this completely ignores the cold start problem.

insights.claim: Elon Musk has done more to advance space conquest than any other individual in the last half-century, yet has personally never been to orbit, illustrating that even the most committed advocates of grand physical engineering projects may derive more actual value from virtual/attention-based activity (e.g., tweeting) than the physical feats they champion.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Cautions against taking founder rhetoric about grand physical ambitions at face value when their own revealed behavior suggests otherwise — relevant to valuing narrative-driven space/deep-tech ventures.
insights.quote: Elon Musk has done far more to conquer space than any other human in the last half century, but he personally has never even been to orbit.
